items.title: ci: add CodSpeed performance benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary

This PR sets up continuous performance measurement with [CodSpeed](https://codspeed.io) for the Bifrost Go modules. It adds a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the existing Go benchmarks on every push to `main` and every pull request, so performance regressions are caught automatically during review.

## Changes

- **`.github/workflows/codspeed.yml`**: New workflow that builds and runs the Go benchmarks under CodSpeed.
  - Uses the **walltime** instrument, which is the mode supported by CodSpeed for Go (it measures real execution time including I/O, threading, and system calls).
  - Runs on `codspeed-macro` runners for stable, bare-metal walltime measurements. These runners are available because `maximhq` is an organization.
  - Authenticates with CodSpeed via OIDC (`id-token: write`), so no token secret is required.
  - Follows the repository conventions: `step-security/harden-runner`, commit-hash-pinned actions, Go `1.26.5` via `actions/setup-go`, and a `concurrency` group to cancel superseded runs.
- **`README.md`**: Added the CodSpeed badge alongside the existing badges.

## Benchmarks measured

The workflow targets the modules whose benchmarks build and run reliably in isolation:

- `core`:
  - `BenchmarkCalculateBackoff`, `BenchmarkIsRateLimitError` (root package)
  - `BenchmarkIsHTMLResponse`, `BenchmarkExtractHTMLErrorMessage` (`providers/utils`)
- `plugins/mocker`:
  - `BenchmarkMockerPlugin_PreHook_SimpleRule`, `_RegexRule`, `_MultipleRules`, `_NoMatch`, `_Template`

Each module is a separate Go module, so benchmarks are invoked per module. Benchmarks are run with `-run '^$'` so only the benchmark functions are measured and the unit test suites (some of which require external MCP servers or provider credentials) are skipped.

## Notes and next steps

- This monorepo contains additional benchmarks in the `framework`, `plugins/governance`, and `transports` modules. Some of those modules currently fail to build against the pinned `core` version (e.g. a `BedrockKeyConfig.BatchRoleARN` schema mismatch) or have long-running, verbose benchmarks, so they were intentionally left out of this initial setup. They can be added incrementally once those modules build cleanly.
- Local verification: the benchmarks were confirmed to compile and run with `go test -bench`. Full CodSpeed walltime instrumentation could not be exercised locally (it requires `perf`/`linux-tools`, which is not available in the setup sandbox); it runs on the `codspeed-macro` runners in CI.

items.title: perf(openai): reduce request-body retention during SSE streaming
items.body:
## Summary

Release serialized request bodies after SSE setup when raw request capture is disabled, instead of retaining them until the stream ends.

Also skip Responses input cleanup when there are no compaction items.

## Changes
- Clear the request-body reference after successful setup in text, chat, and Responses streaming handlers.
- Preserve request bodies for setup errors and when raw capture is enabled.
- Honor the context capture setting when attaching terminal raw requests.
- Skip compaction summary cleanup for inputs without compaction items.
- Add regression tests and benchmarks for raw and structured Go SDK requests.

### Memory measurements

Measured through the Go SDK with structured chat input and raw capture disabled:

| Concurrent streams × input size | Before | After | Saved |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 × 1 MiB | 33.97 MiB | 1.73 MiB | 32.25 MiB |
| 128 × 1 MiB | 134.70 MiB | 5.71 MiB | 128.99 MiB |
| 32 × 4 MiB | 129.97 MiB | 1.72 MiB | 128.25 MiB |

Values are incremental live heap above the idle baseline, measured after GC while all streams remained open. Results are medians of three fresh-process runs per version on Go 1.27.3, darwin/arm64, Apple M2 Pro.

A separate 30-second hold also saved approximately 129 MiB for the 128 × 1 MiB case. With raw capture enabled, heap usage was unchanged.

These measurements use a local mock upstream and exclude the HTTP transport and plugins. They measure live Go heap, not RSS. The benchmark was subsequently simplified to retain only the two SDK paths; the table records the earlier measurements of the same SDK scenarios.

The streaming change adds one capture-setting lookup per stream and no new cache. With capture enabled, the serialized body remains referenced until stream termination.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [x] Refactor
- [ ] Documentation
- [ ] Chore/CI

## Affected areas

- [x] Core (Go)
- [ ] Transports (HTTP)
- [x] Providers/Integrations
- [ ] Plugins
- [ ] UI (React)
- [ ] Docs

## How to test
```sh
cd core

go test ./providers/openai -skip '^TestOpenAI$' -count=1

go test ./providers/openai -run '^$' \
  -bench '^BenchmarkOpenAIConcurrentStreamHeap$/^sdk-typed$/^128x1MiB$/^capture=false$' \
  -benchtime=1x -count=1
```

Local OpenAI unit tests and the concurrent-stream benchmark passed. The 32 × 1 MiB structured SDK case also passed with the race detector. After simplifying the benchmark, both SDK paths were rerun with capture enabled and disabled at 32 × 1 MiB; all four cases passed.

Regression tests cover request-body lifetime, capture overrides, cancellation, billed usage, and compaction cleanup. The new lifetime and allocation tests fail as expected against the pre-change implementation.

Live provider tests were not run. No configuration changes are required.

- [x] No

None.

## Security considerations

Raw request capture continues to follow the existing settings. With capture disabled, the serialized body can be collected before the stream ends.

items.title: [Bug]: Avoid generic JSON decoding for ordinary Gemini/Vertex passthrough stream events
items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched existing issues and discussions to avoid duplicates
- [x] I am using the latest version (or have tested against main/nightly)

### Description

Gemini and Vertex passthrough streaming enables terminal detection in the shared core streaming loop. For each complete event, hasFinishReasonMarker in core/providers/utils/streamterminaldetector.go unmarshals the payload into generic JSON maps and slices to check for completion markers.

Ordinary content events without escapes or terminal-marker text cannot be terminal, yet the current implementation still builds and discards that decoded object graph. This repeats for every such event in a stream.

Terminal detection is required: Gemini/Vertex streams may keep the HTTP body open after emitting a semantic completion event. The suggested optimization should preserve the existing decoding and structural checks whenever a payload could contain a terminal marker; it should not weaken completion, usage, error, or byte-forwarding behavior.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure Gemini or Vertex passthrough with a model-allowed key and a local HTTP mock upstream.
2. Have the upstream return a stream of ordinary candidates[].content.parts[].text events, followed by a terminal finishReason event with usage. Include ordinary usage-bearing events and escaped text in additional cases.
3. Drain the stream and verify the forwarded bytes and final usage.
4. Profile or benchmark terminal detection against the original implementation, using identical inputs and settings. For example, with the local benchmark fixtures:

```
cd core
go test ./providers/utils -run '^$' \
  -bench '^BenchmarkTerminalPayload/GeminiDelta$' -benchmem -count=8
go test . -run '^$' \
  -bench '^BenchmarkGatewayPassthroughStream/Plain$' \
  -benchmem -benchtime=500ms -count=8
```

### Expected behavior

Ordinary marker-free events should avoid constructing a generic JSON object graph solely to determine that no terminal marker is present.  All terminal cases should retain their existing behavior, including escaped marker names, malformed JSON, duplicate keys, candidate completion checks, error envelopes, usage ordering, and early stream completion.

### Actual behavior

In the original implementation, each ordinary event goes through sonic.Unmarshal into any, even when none of the recognized marker spellings or JSON escapes are present. A local audit benchmark measured 18 allocations and about 2,167 bytes per ordinary Gemini event in the predicate before the proposed change.  In an eight-pair local benchmark of a synthetic 256-event stream through Bifrost core and a loopback provider:  - Plain Bifrost SDK stream completion: 860.9 µs → 508.8 µs (about 41% faster); 895,298 → 322,511 bytes/op. - Shared stream loop: 414.2 µs → 162.0 µs (about 61% faster); 695,956 → 149,176 bytes/op.  These results are for a bursty synthetic fixture—not a live provider or production gateway load test. With usage on every event and 25% escaped text, the local SDK-path improvement was smaller: about 21% in elapsed time. Paced-upstream tests showed no convincing completion-time improvement.

### Affected area(s)

Core (Go)

### Version

v2.3.2

### Environment

```text
- OS: Linux 7.2.11-100.fc43.x86_64
- Go: 1.27.2 linux/amd64
- CPU: Intel Core i9-13900H; benchmarks pinned to four physical cores with GOMAXPROCS=4
- Provider calls: Local loopback mock only; no live-provider calls
```

### Relevant logs/output

```shell
A baseline allocation profile of the shared 256-event stream attributed about 79.6% of allocated bytes to the terminal-detection path. The ordinary-event predicate benchmark measured 18 allocations / 2,167 bytes per event before, versus 0 / 0 after the proposed guard.

This is a local benchmark/profile result. Request p50/p99, live-provider latency, HTTP transport overhead, production plugin overhead, and deployment capacity were not measured.
```

### Regression?

No version regression is known. The issue was identified by profiling/benchmarking the existing implementation.

### Severity

Medium (some functionality impaired)

items.title: fix(core): set reasoning from tool plan in cohere non-streaming chat (#9435)
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #9435.

When Cohere answers with tool calls, it returns `message.tool_plan`. The streaming chat path surfaces it as `Delta.Reasoning` (`StreamEventToolPlanDelta` in `core/providers/cohere/chat.go`), but `CohereMessage.ToBifrostChatMessage` previously never read `cm.ToolPlan`. Consequently, non-streaming requests with tool calls returned an assistant message with `tool_calls` and empty content, but with `Reasoning: nil`, dropping the plan that streaming surfaced.

This PR reads non-empty `cm.ToolPlan` during `ToBifrostChatMessage()` conversion, populates `ChatAssistantMessage.Reasoning` and appends an entry to `ReasoningDetails`, merging with any existing thinking blocks.

## Changes

- In `core/providers/cohere/chat.go` (`ToBifrostChatMessage`):
  - Read `cm.ToolPlan != nil && *cm.ToolPlan != ""`
  - Append a `schemas.ChatReasoningDetails` entry of type `schemas.BifrostReasoningDetailsTypeText` with text `cm.ToolPlan`
  - Append `*cm.ToolPlan` to `reasoningText` (concatenating with `\n` if prior `thinking` blocks were present)
  - Existing assistant message creation logic (`if len(reasoningDetails) > 0`) initializes `assistantMessage` if nil and sets `ReasoningDetails` and `Reasoning`.
- In `core/providers/cohere/chat_test.go`:
  - Added unit test `TestToBifrostChatMessage_ToolPlanSetsReasoning` with subtests covering:
    - Tool plan alone with tool calls
    - Tool plan merged with existing thinking block
    - Empty or nil tool plan does not set reasoning
  - Added benchmarks `BenchmarkToBifrostChatMessage_Common` and `BenchmarkToBifrostChatMessage_WithToolPlan`

## Cost on the request flow

- **Common case:** Messages without `ToolPlan` only evaluate a nil-check (`cm.ToolPlan != nil`), adding **0 allocs** and no measurable overhead.
- **Benchmark (`-benchmem` on Intel Core i7-6700K):**
  - Common case (`BenchmarkToBifrostChatMessage_Common`): `~88.5 ns/op`, `80 B/op`, `2 allocs/op`
  - With tool plan (`BenchmarkToBifrostChatMessage_WithToolPlan`): `~533.8 ns/op`, `368 B/op`, `6 allocs/op`


items.title: [fix]: preserve token usage on Responses stream spans
items.body:
Read final-event usage when no plugin accumulates the Responses stream.

Affected packages:
- core/schemas: normalize Responses stream usage and add a regression test and benchmark
- framework/tracing: verify final-event token and cost attributes without accumulation
- core: add a changelog entry

Fixes #8983

## Summary

Responses streams can finish with cost recorded on the span but no token counts when no plugin calls `ProcessStreamingChunk`. Read usage from the final event so spans retain input, output, and total tokens without requiring an accumulated response.

## Changes

- Handle `ResponsesStreamResponse.Response.Usage` in `NormalizedUsage()` using the existing converter.
- Correct the accumulator-only comment; add a focused regression test, benchmark, and changelog entry.
- Add a span-level regression test that supplies final Responses usage without accumulation and asserts input, output, total-token, and cost attributes.

Performance: measured against `dev` at `dc28f7011`, Go 1.27.3, linux/amd64, median of three runs with `-benchmem`, basic usage containing 14/4/18 tokens:

| Final-event normalization | ns/op | B/op | allocs/op |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Before (usage lost) | 13.45 | 0 | 0 |
| After | 186.3 | 192 | 1 |

These results were remeasured after rebasing onto `dev` at `dc28f7011` and supersede the earlier benchmark figures.

Existing response-family cases return before the new branch. The measured case allocates one 192-byte usage object held with the span; optional usage details use the existing converter's copying behavior. No cache or stream-content buffer is added.

After the fix it records 14 input, 4 output, and 18 total tokens, plus cost 0.125. Both package suites pass with the race detector.

items.title: [perf]: optimize passthrough stream terminal detection and cleanup
items.body:
Summary

Reduce unnecessary JSON decoding in the shared passthrough streaming path while preserving terminal detection and safe HTTP connection reuse.

Previously, terminal detection decoded every complete JSON event into generic maps and slices, including ordinary events that could not contain a recognized terminal marker. Stream cleanup could also wait for upstream EOF after semantic completion.

This PR skips decoding only when the payload contains neither recognized marker spellings nor JSON escapes. All uncertain payloads retain the existing decoder and structural checks. Semantic-completion cleanup now performs a bounded HTTP-framing check instead of an unbounded body drain.

Closes #8780.

Changes

  • core/providers/utils/streamterminaldetector.go
    • Add a conservative, allocation-free absence guard.
    • Share existing marker definitions between the guard and structural predicates.
    • Preserve decoding for escaped or marker-bearing payloads, including malformed JSON and duplicate keys.
  • Shared streaming lifecycle and HTTP transport utilities
    • Track semantic completion locally without adding context state or changing public APIs.
    • Deliver final application bytes before potentially delayed HTTP trailers.
    • Confirm HTTP completion before returning a connection to the pool.
    • Bound framing-only cleanup to 10 ms, tightened by the caller’s deadline.
    • Close incomplete, cancelled, malformed, or non-reusable responses rather than pooling them.
  • Regression tests and benchmarks
    • Cover escaped markers, malformed JSON, duplicate keys, fragmented events, usage metadata, cancellation, early completion, and concurrent-stream isolation.
    • Verify completed Vertex TLS connections remain reusable.
    • Add SDK and HTTP gateway benchmarks, including escaped, usage-bearing, JSON-array, paced-upstream, slow-consumer, and concurrent workloads.
    • Update core/changelog.md.

No new dependencies, configuration options, caches, pools, or background goroutines are introduced. Transport changes outside core/ are test-only.

Performance evidence

Final canonical comparison: Go 1.27.3, Linux/amd64, Intel Core i9-13900H, CPU affinity 0,2,4,6, GOMAXPROCS=4, and GOGC=100.

Six fresh-process before/after pairs used alternating execution order and 500 ms benchmark durations. The original production implementation came from the canonical origin/dev branch point, 35899b3. Inputs and byte/usage assertions were equivalent.

Median results for local 256-event streams:

Workload | ns/op before → after | allocs/op before → after | B/op before → after -- | -- | -- | -- SDK, ordinary events | 869,124 → 469,989.5 | 5,955.5 → 1,337 | 842,410.5 → 254,914.5 Supplemental Vertex TLS fixture, ordinary events | 840,116.5 → 465,020 | 5,922 → 1,290 | 875,030.5 → 247,658.5 Supplemental Vertex TLS fixture, mixed usage/escaped events | 1,393,662 → 1,026,763 | 10,587 → 6,158.5 | 1,611,916 → 1,059,305

New TLS connections per operation remained 0 before and after following warm-up.

These are local gateway benchmark-operation measurements, not live-provider latency or request p50/p99. Escaped-event workloads showed overlapping timing ranges and no convincing improvement. Unary allocations remained unchanged; its timing ranges also overlapped. Earlier paced-upstream and slow-consumer measurements showed allocation savings without convincing completion-time gains.

The ordinary-event allocation regression test requires zero allocations in the terminal predicate—not zero allocations for an entire stream.

Type of change

  • [x] Bug fix
  • [ ] Feature
  • [ ] Refactor
  • [ ] Documentation
  • [ ] Chore/CI

Affected areas

  • [x] Core (Go)
  • [x] Transports (HTTP)
  • [x] Providers/Integrations
  • [ ] Plugins
  • [ ] UI (React)
  • [ ] Docs

How to test

Use Go 1.27.3. HTTP integration tests require a Go workspace resolving this branch’s core, framework, and plugin modules locally.

go version

cd core

GOWORK=off go test ./providers/utils -count=1

GOWORK=off go test . ./providers/gemini ./providers/vertex \
  -run 'Test.*Passthrough' -count=1 -timeout=5m

GOWORK=off go test -race . ./providers/utils ./providers/gemini ./providers/vertex \
  -run 'Test(FinishReasonMarker|.*Passthrough.*|ReleaseStreamingResponse|SetupStreamCancellation|StreamCloseUnderActiveReaderIsSafe|IdleTimeoutReader)' \
  -count=1 -timeout=5m

GOWORK=off go test ./providers/utils -run '^$' \
  -fuzz '^FuzzFinishReasonMarkerMatchesReference$' -fuzztime=30s

GOWORK=off go vet . ./providers/utils ./providers/gemini ./providers/vertex

GOWORK=off go test . -run '^$' \
  -bench '^BenchmarkGatewayPassthroughStream$' \
  -benchmem -benchtime=500ms -count=6

cd ../transports

go test ./bifrost-http/integrations -count=1
go vet ./bifrost-http/integrations

go test ./bifrost-http/integrations -run '^$' \
  -bench '^BenchmarkGatewayPassthroughHTTP$' \
  -benchmem -benchtime=500ms -count=6

For before/after comparisons, apply identical benchmark fixtures to the baseline and alternate separate baseline/feature processes; -count=6 alone does not counterbalance execution order.

Completed validation

  • Local core, schemas, key-selection, shared utilities, Gemini, Vertex, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Azure test suites.
  • HTTP integration tests.
  • Focused race checks, go vet, formatting, and diff checks.
  • Coverage-guided differential fuzzing: 708,925 executions over 30 seconds without a mismatch.
  • Benchmark smoke checks against the final staged changes.

Limitations

  • Live-provider tests and deployment-level load tests were not run.
  • Bedrock’s test package has an existing compilation failure: bedrock_test.go:9035:15: undefined: BedrockProvider.
  • HTTP validation used an external temporary workspace and reduced-inlining/stripped-linker flags to accommodate local build limits. Those smoke results are not used for performance claims.

No new configuration or environment variables are required.

Screenshots/Recordings

Not applicable; no UI changes.

Breaking changes

  • [ ] Yes
  • [x] No

No public APIs, request/response schemas, or configuration change. Terminal predicates, byte-exact forwarding, usage accounting, and hook ordering remain unchanged. Semantic completion no longer requires waiting indefinitely for upstream EOF.

Related issues

Closes #8780.

Security considerations

Authentication, authorization, credential handling, and provider routing are unchanged.

A byte match never establishes terminal completion; it only permits the existing decoding and structural validation. Connections are reused only after validated HTTP completion. Cancellation and incomplete-response paths continue to discard connections.

Checklist

  • [x] I reviewed the contribution guidelines in docs/contributing/raising-a-pr.mdx and docs/contributing/code-conventions.mdx
  • [x] I added/updated tests where appropriate
  • [x] I updated documentation where needed through code comments and the core changelog

items.title: [fix]: bill and govern Anthropic advisor iterations
items.body:
## Summary

Anthropic advisor sub-inferences can name a model different from the executor. Their `usage.iterations` entries were not included in request pricing, and the advisor model was not checked against virtual-key access rules.

This applies the published [advisor-iteration patch](https://github.com/AntibodyEvaluation/Zeroday-Evaluation/blob/main/bifrost/Vulnerability/ZD-2026-BIFROST-ADVISOR-ITERATION-RESIDUAL/report/advisory/patch/0001-bill-and-admit-anthropic-advisor-iterations.patch), with regression tests, benchmarks, harness cases, and changelog entries. In the synthetic pricing fixture, executor cost is $0.002 and advisor cost is $0.030: the corrected total is $0.032 rather than $0.002.

## Changes

- Preserve Anthropic iteration usage in unary and streaming passthrough responses, retaining the latest cumulative breakdown through `message_stop`.
- Price `advisor_message` iterations using the advisor model. Do not bill executor iterations twice or trust provider-reported iteration cost. If advisor pricing is unavailable, fall back to executor pricing; this is an estimate, not a guarantee of the provider's exact charge.
- Evaluate advisor models from Responses tools and passthrough JSON through the existing governance checks. Existing protection refuses body-model limits that the outer request cannot settle.
- Add four admission harness cases: native `/anthropic/v1/messages` and `/v1/responses`, each with streaming and non-streaming requests. Each case creates and removes its own restricted virtual key.

The covered paths are direct Anthropic Responses and native passthrough, in both modes. This change does not add advisor support to Chat Completions or expand provider compatibility. Advisor egress through Bedrock, Vertex, or Azure was not validated.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix

## Affected areas

- [x] Core (Go)
- [x] Providers/Integrations
- [x] Plugins
- Framework model pricing and provider-harness tests

## Validation

Tested with Go 1.27.3 on Linux/arm64, using a workspace linking the local core, framework, and governance modules.

- Before applying the implementation patch, the new pricing and admission tests failed on assertions: advisor cost was omitted, and restricted keys were allowed across all four paths.
- After applying the patch, the same regressions passed.
- The full `framework/modelcatalog/datasheet` and `plugins/governance` unit suites passed.
- Targeted Anthropic usage, conversion, passthrough, and streaming tests passed, including cache-read token preservation and repeated cumulative iteration events.
- Harness augmentation and filtering passed, selecting exactly four new cases.
- `gofmt` and `git diff --check` passed.

Commands used from the repository root with the local Go workspace:

```sh
go test ./framework/modelcatalog/datasheet ./plugins/governance -count=1
go test ./core/providers/anthropic -run 'Test(ExtractAnthropicPassthroughUsage|AnthropicPassthroughStreamUsage|PassthroughPreservesAdvisorIterations|BillableAnthropicUsage|ConvertAnthropicUsageToBifrostUsage|PassthroughStream_CompactionIterations)' -count=1
```

The live provider harness, full application/UI builds, and repository-wide CI were not run. No paid model calls were made.

## Request-path cost

Baseline: `369d68434759f44caa911b2215a03ef521575d7f` with the benchmark tests added, before applying the implementation patch. Values below are medians of three 100 ms runs in the same local Linux/arm64 VM; short-run latency and pooled-parser byte counts were noisy, so these are measurements rather than statistically significant performance claims.

| Benchmark | ns/op before → after | B/op before → after | allocs/op before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Passthrough extraction, no advisor | 1,334 → 1,964 | 940 → 962 | 7 → 7 |
| Passthrough extraction, advisor | 2,984 → 3,915 | 1,590 → 2,514 | 13 → 16 |
| Cost calculation, no advisor | 3,513 → 3,626 | 2,848 → 2,848 | 14 → 14 |
| Cost calculation, advisor | 4,451 → 5,973 | 2,848 → 5,952 | 14 → 31 |
| Governance hook, no advisor | 10,249 → 9,462 | 5,433 → 5,433 | 118 → 118 |
| Governance hook, advisor | 9,736 → 17,401 | 5,433 → 8,169 | 118 → 209 |

```sh
go test ./core/providers/anthropic ./framework/modelcatalog/datasheet ./plugins/governance -run '^$' -bench 'Benchmark(ExtractAnthropicPassthroughAdvisorUsage|CalculateCostAdvisorIterations|PreLLMHookAdvisorModels)$' -benchmem -benchtime=100ms -count=3
```

No-advisor allocation counts remain unchanged in these fixtures; the passthrough usage struct gains a slice header. Advisor requests allocate iteration conversion/pricing data and perform another governance evaluation. The stream accumulator retains only the latest provider iteration slice, replacing it when a newer non-empty breakdown arrives. Its size follows the provider's iteration list and its lifetime is the stream; no global cache or cross-request retention is introduced.

## Breaking changes

No configuration or request-schema migration is required. Requests naming an advisor model outside a virtual key's permissions are now rejected, and recorded request costs include advisor iterations.

## Security considerations

This closes an advisor-model admission gap and omitted advisor accounting in the covered paths. It uses the existing governance evaluator and body-model limit safeguards. Test data contains synthetic tokens and pricing only.

## Checklist

items.title: [fix]: Gemini provider - replay extra_content.google.thought_signature instead of the skip sentinel
items.body:
## Summary

When a chat request with tool-call history goes to the native `gemini` provider, `convertBifrostMessagesToGemini` recovers a replayed function call's thought signature only from the `<call_id>_ts_<base64url>` id suffix and from `reasoning_details`. Anything else gets `skip_thought_signature_validator`. `ChatAssistantMessageToolCall.ExtraContent` carries `extra_content.google.thought_signature`, the field Google's own OpenAI-compatible endpoint uses, but the Gemini request converter never reads it. A client that does the right thing and sends the signature back as `extra_content` therefore gets its real signature replaced by the sentinel (case P1 of #8149).

## Changes

- `core/providers/gemini/utils.go`: new `thoughtSignatureFromExtraContent`, which reads `google.thought_signature` (base64) from the tool call's `extra_content`. It is tried after the id suffix and `reasoning_details`, and before the sentinel, so requests that already carried a signature behave as before, and requests with neither still get the sentinel.
- `core/providers/gemini/thoughtsignatureextracontent_test.go`: tests and benchmark (below).
- `core/changelog.md`: entry added.

Not changed: the sentinel for history without any signature (P3, P4, P5, P7 in the issue), the Responses converter (`responses.go`, whose tool messages have no `extra_content`), and the Anthropic and genai inbound paths (P5, P6). Those need design decisions the issue leaves open.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix

## Affected areas

- [x] Core (Go)
- [x] Providers/Integrations

## How to test

```sh
cd core
go test ./providers/gemini/ -run 'ExtraContentThoughtSignature|NoSignatureStillGetsTheSentinel|UnusableExtraContent' -count=1
go test ./providers/gemini/ -count=1
go test ./providers/gemini/ -run '^$' -bench ExtraContentThoughtSignature -benchmem -count=3
```

`TestConvertBifrostMessagesToGemini_ExtraContentThoughtSignatureIsReplayed` (new) replays the issue's P1 request and expects the decoded signature in the outgoing function-call part. It fails on `dev` (the sentinel is written) and passes now. Two more cases check that history without a signature still gets the sentinel, and that unusable `extra_content` (no `thought_signature`, invalid base64, a different top-level key) falls back to it. The whole `providers/gemini` package passes and `go vet` is clean. The Go tests ran on golang:1.26 with the `go` directive of a temporary module file lowered to 1.26, since `go.mod` asks for 1.27.2.

Benchmark (`BenchmarkConvertBifrostMessagesToGemini_ExtraContentThoughtSignature`, a three-message history with one tool call carrying the field, `-count=3`):

| | ns/op | B/op | allocs/op |
|---|---|---|---|
| dev | 1359 – 1414 | 1732 – 1739 | 24 |
| this PR | 1593 – 1661 | 1785 – 1790 | 25 |

The extra allocation is the decoded signature, which is the work the request needs and which `dev` skipped by writing the sentinel. Calls without `extra_content` return before any parsing.

## Breaking changes

- [x] No

## Related issues

Refs #8149 (fixes its P1 case only, so the issue stays open for the rest).

## Security considerations

None.

## Checklist

- [x] I read `docs/contributing/README.md` and followed the guidelines
- [x] I added/updated tests where appropriate
- [ ] I updated documentation where needed (n/a)
- [x] I verified builds succeed (Go and UI) (Go only; no UI change)
- [ ] I verified the CI pipeline passes locally if applicable

This change was made with Claude Code; the tests and the benchmark above were run on dev and on this branch.

items.title: fix: convert off spec stop reasons to provider standard for oai and anthropic integration
items.body:
## Summary

Providers such as vLLM and Bedrock emit finish/stop reasons that neither the Anthropic nor the OpenAI spec defines (`repetition`, `abort`, `guardrail_intervened`, `content_filter`). Strict SDK clients can fail on these values. This PR maps them to the nearest spec-defined value on the Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible wire formats.

## Changes

- **Anthropic stop reasons:** Added mappings to the stop-reason table so Anthropic clients only see defined values:
  - `content_filter` and `guardrail_intervened` map to `refusal` (Bedrock guardrails).
  - `repetition` and `abort` map to `end_turn` (vLLM repetition detection and engine abort).
- **OpenAI-compatible routes:** Added `openAIOffSpecFinishReason` and `openAISpecFinishReasons`, wired into `openAIWireCostResponse` for chat and text completion responses (including streaming chunks):
  - `repetition` and `abort` map to `stop`.
  - `guardrail_intervened` maps to `content_filter`.
  - Spec-defined reasons (`stop`, `length`, `tool_calls`, `content_filter`) pass through unchanged.
- **No mutation of shared responses:** Choices are copied only when a rewrite is needed, so the original response keeps its raw finish reason. The `/v1` route serializes the Bifrost response directly and keeps the raw value.
- **Low overhead on the common path:** The copy happens only when an off-spec reason is found, so spec-defined reasons add no allocation. A benchmark compares the common path with the rewrite path.
- **Tests:**
  - New Anthropic cases cover `content_filter` taking precedence over `incomplete_details`, `guardrail_intervened`, `repetition`, and `abort`.
  - A new OpenAI route test covers chat, chat stream, text, and text stream, and asserts the source response is not mutated.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix

```sh
# UI

pnpm i || npm i

```

items.title: feat(core): per-request timeout override via BifrostContextKeyRequestTimeout
items.body:
## Summary

Adds a per-request upstream timeout override, `BifrostContextKeyRequestTimeout`. A caller can now replace the provider's `default_request_timeout_in_seconds` for a single request. This helps calls that need longer than the provider-wide timeout (reasoning models, image or video generation, cold starts) and calls that should fail sooner. Previously the timeout was fixed per client or transport, so the only way to change it was to build a separate client.

The override is a per-attempt limit, like the provider timeout it replaces. An attempt that exceeds it fails as a provider timeout, and Bifrost moves on to the next fallback. The context deadline remains the budget for the whole request across retries and fallbacks, and it still caps every attempt. A context deadline alone does not lift the provider timeout.

## Changes

- Added the `BifrostContextKeyRequestTimeout` context key (`time.Duration`) and a `GetRequestTimeout(ctx, fallback)` helper. It returns the override when it is set and positive, and the provider default otherwise. It never replaces the ctx deadline.
- fasthttp context transport: `RoundTrip` now uses the override in place of the client's `WriteTimeout` and `ReadTimeout` for that request. The override can lengthen or shorten the timeout, and the ctx deadline still caps it.
- Added `DoHTTPRequestWithTimeout` for net/http clients. It replaces `http.Client.Timeout` and `http.Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout`, which cannot vary per request.
  - Unary calls (`boundBody=true`) bound headers and body.
  - Streaming calls (`boundBody=false`) bound only the wait for response headers. After that, the stream idle timeout applies.
  - The attempt context is released when the response body is closed. The hook sits inside `upstreamTimingBody`, so `NewIdleTimeoutReader` can still unwrap it.
- Bedrock:
  - Removed the fixed `Client.Timeout` and `ResponseHeaderTimeout` from its clients and transports.
  - The provider now stores `requestTimeout` and applies it per attempt through `DoHTTPRequestWithTimeout`.
  - Switched the unary, streaming, file, batch, model-listing, passthrough and Nova Sonic realtime paths over to the new helper.
- Runway: `pollRunwayTask` now uses the override as its polling window instead of always using `default_request_timeout_in_seconds`.
- Documented the key in the Go SDK context-keys quickstart, with a usage example and a reference table row.
- Tests and benchmarks:
  - New tests cover the helper, the fasthttp transport (extend, shorten, deadline cap, no override), the Bedrock unary and stream paths, Runway polling, and the failure-class ladder (an override timeout is a provider timeout that falls back).
  - New benchmarks compare the old fixed timeouts with the per-request mechanism.

## Type of change

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Documentation
- [ ] Chore/CI

## Affected areas

- [x] Core (Go)
- [ ] Transports (HTTP)
- [x] Providers/Integrations
- [ ] Plugins
- [ ] UI (React)
- [x] Docs

## How to test

Run the core tests, including the new timeout tests and benchmarks:

```sh
# Core/Transports
go version
go test ./core/providers/utils/... ./core/providers/bedrock/... ./core/providers/runway/...
go test ./core/...
go test ./core/providers/utils -run xxx -bench 'HTTPUnaryTimeout|HTTPStreamHeaderTimeout|Transport_Buffered'
```

Expected outcomes:
- With a 1s provider timeout and a 1.5s upstream, Bedrock unary and stream requests time out by default.
- With `BifrostContextKeyRequestTimeout` set to 3s, the same requests succeed.
- A ctx deadline shorter than the override still ends the request with `RequestTimedOut`.
- A 100ms override ends Runway polling quickly even when the provider timeout is 300s.

To try the override in the SDK:

```go
bfCtx := schemas.NewBifrostContext(context.Background(), time.Now().Add(15*time.Minute))
bfCtx.SetValue(schemas.BifrostContextKeyRequestTimeout, 10*time.Minute)
```

## Screenshots/Recordings

N/A

## Breaking changes

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

Without the override, behavior is unchanged: the provider's `default_request_timeout_in_seconds` still bounds each attempt.

## Related issues

N/A

## Security considerations

No auth, secrets or PII changes. The override is bounded by the ctx deadline, so a caller cannot extend a request beyond its overall budget.

- [x] I added/updated tests where appropriate
- [x] I updated documentation where needed
- [ ] I verified builds succeed (Go and UI)
- [ ] I verified the CI pipeline passes locally if applicable
